text:
Droit de la famille — 232098

2023 QCCS 4801

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF GATINEAU

N
o
:

550-04-021537-218

DATE :

December
15, 2023

______________________________________________________________________

BY THE HONOURABLE RENÉE THÉRIAULT,
J.C.S.

______________________________________________________________________

S. M.

Applicant

v.

H. H.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

OVERVIEW

[1]

The Applicant (the mother)
and the Defendant (the father) separated three years ago.  They are the
parents of two young children, a six-year boy (child X) and a four-year old boy
(child Y).

[2]

The mother seeks exclusive
parenting time over the children and requests that they be barred from any
form of access to the father due to his past violent and abusive behaviour.
The father consents to the mother’s request for exclusive parenting time but seeks
unsupervised access with the children on a gradual basis, including overnight
access from Friday to Monday, two out of every three weekends.

[3]

The father’s access to the
children has been provisionally subject to supervision since February 2021
pending the present judgment.  In October 2022, pursuant to a court-ordered
psychological assessment, it was
recommended
that contact between the father and the
children be maintained every two weeks for two hours under supervision and
that the father continue to pursue parental counseling.

[4]

The trial proceeded
over a four-day period
on October
10-13, 2023.  During the trial, the parties settled the financial aspects of
their dispute, agreeing to the modalities applicable to child support and
division of property.  As indicated, it was also during the trial that the
father consented to the mother’s request for
exclusive parenting time of the children.

[5]

The only remaining issues
are whether all contact between the father and the children should be
severed, as per the mother’s request, or whether supervision over the
father’s access rights should be lifted, as per the father’s request.

The Court must also
determine whether the mother, in light of the circumstances, it entitled to
extrajudicial costs and punitive damages.

[6]

For the following reasons,
the Court has concluded that the recommendations drawn by the expert pursuant
to the court-ordered psychological assessment should be followed.  In
reaching this conclusion, the Court has determined that it would be premature
at this time to sever all contact between the father and the children.  By
the same token, the Court has likewise determined that it would be premature
to lift supervision over the father’s access rights.

[7]

The Court accordingly concludes
that the father’s access to the children should remain in place at regular
two-week intervals for two hours under supervision.  The Court further
recommends that going forward, (i) the children be supported by a therapist
to monitor the impact on their well-being of the supervised visits with their
father, both before and after the visits, and that (ii) the father continue
to pursue parental counselling sessions.

CONTEXT

[8]

The parties met online in
2015 while living in Town A.  Their eldest son, six year-old child X, was born in
Town A on [...], 2017.  Their younger son, four year-old child Y, was born in Town
B on [...], 2019.

[9]

The parties’ relationship cam
to end following repeated episodes of violent and abusive behaviour on the part
of the father.  The mother first reported the father’s behaviour to the police
in 2019 when the parties were living in Town A.  This led to criminal charges
against the father, specifically for assaulting child X and uttering death
threats towards the mother.

[10]

After reporting the father’s behaviour to the
police, the mother temporarily left the family home for a period of three
months.  During this period, she lived in a women’s shelter but remained in
contact with the father.  She moved back to the family home following an
apology on his part as well as an undertaking to attend counselling.
Subsequently, she withdrew her statement to the police, resulting in the charges
being dropped.

[11]

The family later moved to Town C, which is where
the parties and their children were living when the pandemic hit.  During this
period, the mother was on maternity leave from her job as a kitchen designer,
and the father, who works as a chef, lost his job.  This was a particularly volatile
time in the family home, so much so that at the parties’ request, the father’s
parents came to live with them for a period of approximately six months.

[12]

During the pandemic, the father’s violent and abusive
behaviour persisted, and the mother made the decision to definitively end the
relationship.  This decision brought on a particularly violent incident which
resulted in the father being removed from the home by the police in December
2020.  Criminal charges were laid against the father following the mother’s
statement to the police, specifically for assault and threats towards child X, as
well as towards her and the father’s mother.  These charges remain pending, and
a criminal trial date has been set for 2024.  A no contact order is in place
prohibiting the father from contacting the mother and the children except as
otherwise permitted by the Court in the context of the parties’ family law
proceedings.

[13]

The family law proceedings were initiated by the
mother.  On February 2, 2021, Justice Suzanne Tessier rendered an interim
judgement granting the mother custody of both children and granting the father supervised
access rights at [Organisation A] (hereinafter [Organisation A]) in Town C once
a week for a period not exceeding 2 hours.  The father was also ordered to pay
400$ per month in child support.

[14]

Four months later, on June 22,
2021, Justice Marie-Josée Bédard ordered, with the parties’ consent, a
psychosocial assessment in view of assisting the Court with their dispute
regarding the children.

[15]

On August 4, 2021, Justice Pierre Isabelle denied
the mother’s application to suspend the father’s access to the children, and
accordingly maintained the father’s supervised access rights at [Organisation
A] once a week for a period not exceeding 2 hours.

[16]

On October 19, 2021, upon
further application by the mother, Justice Anne-France Gagnon temporarily
suspended the
father’s supervised access rights.
At this juncture, the mother had moved with
the children from Town C to Town D (Ontario), where she now lives with her new
partner and their then-newborn daughter.

[17]

Two weeks later, on November
2, 2021, Justice Gagnon rejected the mother’s request to suspend the
father’s supervised access rights and accordingly renewed the father’s
supervised access rights at [Organisation A] once a week for a period not
exceeding 2 hours.  Justice Gagnon also ordered that the father arrive 15
minutes earlier than the mother before each visit and wait a further 15 minutes
at the end of each visit.

[18]

On March 8, 2022, Justice
Dominique Goulet renewed the interim judgements then in effect until September
7, 2022.

[19]

Likewise, on September 12,
2022, Justice Jean Faullem renewed the interim judgements then in effect until
November 29, 2022, and in so doing rejected the father’s motion to lift
supervision over his access with the children as well as his request for dinner
with them once a week.

[20]

On October 18, 2022,
pursuant to the court-ordered psychological assessment, an expert report was
filed
recommending
that contact between the father and the children be
maintained every two weeks for two hours under supervision and that the father
continue to pursue parental counseling.

[21]

On February 28, 2023, Justice Carole Therrien
ordered, upon application of the mother and citing the expert report, that the father’s
supervised access rights be exercised every two weeks at the [Organisation B] in
Town D.  Justice Therrien also permitted the father to request continued
supervised visits at [Organisation A] in Town C provided third-party transport
was available.  In addition, she ordered virtual visits between the father and
the children via [Organisation A] pending arrangements regarding in-person
visits at the [Organisation B] which resumed in April 2023.

[22]

On June 6, 2023, Justice Therrien dismissed the
father’s application seeking weekly supervised visits, but confirmed his supervised
access rights every two weeks at the [Organisation B].

[23]

On August 2, 2023, Justice Goulet dismissed the
father’s application for an additional psychosocial assessment given that a
trial date had been set for October 2023.

THE EVIDENCE

[24]

During the trial, the Court
heard testimony from the expert who conducted the court-ordered psychosocial
assessment, both at the outset of the trial and again at the end in order to
respond to additional questions on the part of the Court regarding the implications
of the expert’s recommendations.  The Court also heard extensive testimony on
the part of both the mother and the father.  A summary of the expert evidence
as well as of the testimony delivered by the mother and father is set forth
next.

The
Expert Evidence

[25]

In presenting her report, the expert emphasizes
that her assessment is aimed at “defining the appropriate custody and
visitation planning for the child that would be in the child’s best interest”,
it being understood that the expert undertook her evaluation in connection with
both children at issue.

[26]

As part of her report, the expert specifies that
she spoke with the mother, first over the phone and subsequently in person, and
likewise had a telephone conversation with the father before meeting him in
person, in both instances back in September 2022.  The expert also consulted
the [Organisation A] reports detailing the father’s supervised visits with the
children as well as witness documentation.  In addition, she consulted the
school safety plan in place for child X and, importantly, she had a telephone
meeting with child X’s trauma therapist.

[27]

Thereafter, the expert observed the father with
the children during a supervised visit at [Organisation A], and she also
observed the mother with the children at their home.  Furthermore, the expert
met with the mother’s new partner and with child X himself.  Finally, she
consulted videos and recordings provided by the mother.  The entire assessment
process undertaken by the expert stretched over a one-month period and resulted
in a comprehensive 18-page report detailing the expert’s observations.  The
Court considers it important to reproduce these observations in extenso and
with the required emphasis given their relevance to the parties’ remaining
dispute regarding the father’s access to the children.

[28]

From the outset, based on her meeting with the
father, the expert notes the following with respect to his relationship with
the children (emphasis added):

Mr. H. mentions that he is
a good father but does not know how to parent since he was never able to. He
mentions that when
[child X]

was born, he had a hard time breastfeeding and cried a lot from hunger. Mr. H. was
working three different jobs and was very tired.
He admits saying that he
wanted to throw the baby against the wall and that he hated him.
He
justifies that he was exhausted, as any father would be.

Mr. H. explains that he
has never laid a finger on
[child Y]
.
However,
he has spanked
[child X]
.
When we asked the frequency, Mr. H. responded “well I spanked him”. During our
meeting, he mentions that he has only tapped
[child
X]
on the cheek. However, throughout
our conversation, Mr. H. mentioned “oh after I smacked
[child
X]
in the face, I brought him to his
room”.
He also admits pulling his ear and
yanking his winter suit. When we question Mr. H. in regards to the situation in
which
[child X]
tripped over his foot,
Mr. H. explains that he got upset and put him in his room. We questioned if he
prohibited the mother from going to see him and Mr. H. said “probably, but it
was his consequence and I was punishing him”.

Mr. H. admits that he
threatened
[child X]

to put feces in his face if he did not use the potty.

Mr. H. explains that
[child X]

would cry but this was a joke and not to take seriously.

As for name calling, Mr. H.
admits that he called
[child X]

names behind his back frequently.
He admits saying that he is retarded and a
wild animal that needs to be locked up.
He mentions that he was stressed
and had a headache when he expressed that. To
[child
X]
’s face, he claims that he has only said “I am so sick and
tired of your shit” repeatedly.

As a parent now, Mr. H. expresses
that he has changed. He has also followed and completed a parenting class. He
explains that he has gained tools on how to stay calm and use his words. He
adds that he believes
[child X]
is
jealous of
[child Y]
.
He noticed that in the visits,
[child X]

pushed
[child Y]
out of the way to give
him a hug first. Mr. H. mentions that he believes this is happening because
[child
X]
wants to impress him.

[29]

Having attended a supervised access visit of the
children with the father, the expert further observes the following (emphasis
added):

During the first 25
minutes of the visits with their father,
[child X] was shut down
and saying that he was upset.  The father repeated numerous times what is wrong
and [child X] kept responding “I don’t know, I am mad at you, I don’t like you,
this is boring”.  The father kept asking why but [child X] kept repeating the
same things.  We also noticed that when Mr. H. ask the children to do something
such as wash their hands or to stop making loud noises, or to not eat the chocolate
bar both of them did not listen.  Instead, [child X] decided to lick the
chocolate off of his hands and Mr. H. went and got wipes to wash their hands
instead.
Mr. H. demonstrated passive parenting
style and lacked consistency.  However, there were many moments where the
children were enjoying the visit when they played foosball (
sic
) and
watched videos on his phone.  We believe that Mr. H. would benefit from
continuing parenting class to learn how to properly intervene, especially that
his relationship with [child X] is evidently fragile.

[30]

Regarding the supervised visits, the expert
refers to the [Organisation A] reports and points out the following:

These documents confirm
that the father has repeatedly expressed that he does not want his sons to call
the mother’s new boyfriend “daddy” and finds this inappropriate.  In fact, on
the visit of December 10
th
2021, Mr. H… tells
[child
X] that he is not aloud (
sic
) to call Ma. Dad.  The facilitator asked
him to change the subject since he was holding [child X] in his arms and
forcing him to look at him.  The father continued to repeat, “I am your only
father”.

[31]

The expert also met with child X, who was then five-years
old, and reports the following (emphasis added):

Even though his
integration in school was difficult at the beginning, major progress in his
behaviours has been expressed.  During our assessment, we noticed that [child
X] is very sweet, loving and developing well following his therapy and
intervention plan.  It is important to note that when we met with [child X], it
was difficult to keep his attention since he was reluctant to “meet with a stranger”.

However, once we began to talk, he was able to express that he does not like
going to see his father, he makes him mad and scared but he does not know why.

He expressed that he would like to keep the same amount of visits but no
more.  When we questioned [child X] about the past, or where he lived before, [child
X] immediately shut down and said he did not want to talk about it.
When
we questioned in regards to his new home,
[child X] expressed that
his mother and his dad (Mr. D.) make him happy.

During our assessment, [child
Y] was seen as playful and sweet.  He is 2 years old and attends daycare.  Like
we mentioned above, due to his young age, [child Y] does not show any signs of
anxiety or fear in regards to his father.  However, it was noticed that the
bond between he and his brother is strong; they support each other, encourage
each other and get alone (
sic
) well which, according to Mrs. M. and Mr. D.
was not present in the past.

[32]

Importantly, the expert spoke with child X’s trauma therapist who shared her insight (emphasis added):

Mrs. Borschevsky explains
that she had follow-ups with
[child X]

from December 2021 to June 2022. They had 18, sessions together which was based
on
[child X]
’s trauma with his father.

She explains that during the sessions, when
[child
X]
would speak about his past and
“scary stories” were all based from the father.
At
the time, the therapist,
[child X]
’s
teacher’s and his mother were all concerned in regards to his violent
behaviour. He would use words that were not appropriate for his age as well as
name calling. He also was very physically violent towards his mother when he
was upset.
The therapist clarifies that her interventions were on Wednesdays
and she therefore was not able to evaluate
[child
X]
state before or after seeing his father.

However, when she would ask about his supervised visitation with him,
[child
X]
would shut down, and use avoidance. He would also start
fidgeting and show signs of anxiety as well as discomfort. The therapist was
also able to give the mother proper tools for her to be able to help
[child
X]
’s aggressive behaviours.
By the end of their follow-ups,
it was noticed by the mother as well as the school, the major improvements in
his behaviours.

[33]

At the time of the expert’s assessment, the parties
had been separated for nearly two years and the children’s contact with their
father had consisted of supervised visits on a weekly basis.  The expert makes
the following evaluation in this regard (emphasis added):

Since the couple’s
separation, the mother has had full custody and the father has had supervised
visits every Friday morning.  According to the therapist, the mother and the
school staff, at the beginning of the separation,
[child
X]
was demonstrating intense violent behaviours towards his
peers and mother.  In fact, he was showing many behaviours that the father
admits doing to his son, such as name-calling and physical consequences.
According to the therapist,
[child X]

had improved immensely at the end of their follow-ups in June 2022.
We
question if this major improvements is not only from the therapy, but from the
decrease contacts with his father.

[Child X]

and
[child Y]
are currently developing
well in their new home.  Even though Mr. H. has expressed that he is displeased
with
[child X]
calling Mr. D. dad, we do
not see this as harmful for the child.  To add, we noticed that Mr. D.’s implication
in this family is positive and healthy.
In this case, we evaluate that the
father’s anger is personal and is not for the child’s best interest.
To
clarify, the bond between the children and the mother’s partner is separate
from the bond they have with their father.  It is important to respect their
relationship, for the child’s mental health.

[34]

Overall, based on her observations, the
expert recommends that supervision over the father’s access to the children
should remain in place for the following reasons (emphasis added):

During our assessment,
both parents described a very difficult past together. The mother describes the
father as verbally and physically abusive towards the children and herself. She
mentions that she was the victim in this situation and was suffering from the
cycle of woman abuse. There has been may worrisome conflicts between the
couple, which involved the police, and the necessity for Mrs. M. to live in a
woman shelter. Mr. H. expresses the same conflicts, partially admitted his
faults but also excused his behaviour by saying he was over worked, tired, or
that everyone had it out for him. Even though the version of the couple’s
history significantly differs from one parent to another, the psychosocial
assessment was requested by the court to evaluate their parental abilities and
not to find out who is the victim in the situation.

That being said, Mr. H. admits
physically abusing
[child X]
.
He admits spanking him, threatening to put faeces (
sic
) in his face,
giving harsh consequences, having unrealistic expectations towards his son and
calling him names. He also admits saying he wanted to throw him against the
wall as well as wanting to put a knife through his head, both times he was left
alone with him for a longer period of time. Even though Mr. H. has completed a
parenting class, we question if he has truly grasped the severity of his
actions due to his excuses expressed during our assessment. We noticed a lack
of empathy and belittling the situations.
He
also expressed that his parents beat him and used colourful language growing up
and he therefore does not see the issue.
We also noticed that these were not
isolated events, but repetitive. Numerous times during our assessment, Mr. H. expressed
liking to be in control in different types of situation.
He mentions that
his OCD “makes him this way” and that he does not see an issue in correcting
woman and children in regards to the way they walk, place their shoes etc. It
as reported that
[child X]
was
having a hard time knowing how to “free play” at school. We question if this is
because his father tried to control too excessively. Mr. H. also does not have
a current employment or the material necessary to welcome his children at his
home.
We believe that the supervision in a facility remains necessary in
this case.

[35]

In addition, the expert makes the
following recommendation regarding the frequency and location of the father’s
visits with the children, as well as whether they should be attended by both
children together (emphasis added):

To add, according to the
trauma based therapist as well as the schools documents,
[child
X]
was showing extreme behaviour difficulty. He would use words
that were not appropriate for his age as well as name-calling. He also was very
physically violent towards his mother when he was upset. He would also show
signs of anxiety when asked about the supervised visitations with his father.
We
question if the frequency of these visits are affecting
[child
X]
in a negative way. We also noticed
that the relationship between
[child X]

and his father is fragile during our observation. During our meeting with
[child
X]
as well as during the observation
with his father,
[child X]

expresses that he does not like him and that he is scared.
[child
X]
demonstrates signs of past trauma
after the visits with his father as well as a few days following contacts such
as having night terrors, being angry, sad, keeping to himself and hard to
approach.
Furthermore, the child has to travel
during his school hours, which can put him behind in his academic progress.
We
believe that changing the visitations to every second Saturday or Sunday
mornings would benefit the child. We also believe that moving the supervised
visitation to the [Organisation B] in which the mother has already applied for,
would also benefit the children to avoid them from being in the car for long
period of hours.
Even though there has been less abuse reported towards
[child
Y]
due to his younger age,
we believe that keeping the
children together during the visits would be in their best interest due to the
prior conflict between the brothers that was established when the father was
present in the home
.

[36]

Significantly, the expert concludes her report by
indicating that while supervision remains necessary, the children should not be
prevented from seeing their father altogether.  Hence, she is of the view that
the father should continue to have access to the children, albeit under
supervision (emphasis added):

During our observation, we
noticed that the mother has good parental skills and bond with her children.
Mr. D. also demonstrates a strong healthy bond with the boys.  They have
everything they need to support them.
Even though the mother requested a no
contact between the father and their children, Mr. H. has never missed a
visitation and even though it has been reported that he was inappropriate
towards the children in regards to calling [the mother’s new partner] dad, he
does have positive visitations with them while being supervised with
professionals.  We thus believe that there should remain a supervised contact
between the children and their father to continue working on their
relationship.

[37]

At trial, the expert added that while a year has
passed since her report, her recommendations remain the same.  Specifically,
she remains of the view that it would not be in the interest of the children to
sever all contact with the father.  She also remains of the view that
supervision is still necessary for the time being.  While she acknowledges that
supervision is normally meant to be a short-term measure, she states that this
case is an exception to the rule and that supervision is required for the
foreseeable future.  In the expert’s opinion, a true change in the father’s
behaviour and parental skills will require significant time and effort on his
part.

[38]

The Court now turns to the testimony given by the parents.  The Court does so
again extensively, noting that the observations made by the expert are entirely
consistent with their respective testimony.

The Mother’s Testimony

[39]

The mother testifies that she lives in fear of
the father due the physical and emotional abuse she and the children endured
during their relationship.  Based on the traumatizing effect of this abuse, she
is of the view that all visits with the father should cease altogether.  She
emphasizes that the visits result in emotional deregulation on the part of child
X, and a lack of desire to pursue the visits on the part of child Y.  In
essence, the mother claims that it is unsafe for the children to pursue their visits
with the father, even under supervision, due to the impact of these visits on
them.  She is of the view that no amount of therapy will assist the father with
his parenting skills given that his past efforts in this regard have in her
opinion been unfruitful.  She accordingly requests that the children’s visits
with the father, and hence any contact with him, be terminated going forward.

[40]

As part of her testimony, the mother indicates
that she has made it her job to protect her children and feels that the job
will never be fully done.  She feels permanently traumatized by her
relationship with the father.  She adds that she has suffered since her late
teens from bouts of anxiety which has required medication and that her anxiety
increased during her relationship with the father.  She describes her
relationship with him as toxic from very early on.  She was in her early
twenties when she met him, at a time when she was feeling lonely in a new city
(Town A) where she had been transferred for work.  She states that he was
controlling, hurtful, disrespectful and critical of her appearance, and refers
to a pattern of unfaithful sexual behaviour on his part.  The mother testifies
that the father’s abusive behaviour escalated once they had their first child,
exacerbated by alcohol and substance abuse, including cocaine.

[41]

When describing the father’s behaviour more
generally, the mother indicates that it goes beyond a “standard
case of violence” given the father’s extreme, controlling and unapologetic
personality. She notes that his aggressive forms of
communication were also at play between the father and his parents, that the
father had a particularly aggressive attitude towards his own mother, and
likewise towards her mother as well.

[42]

Corroborating the expert evidence and the
father’s admissions in this regard, the mother explains that the father was
abusive with child X very soon after his birth, expressing anger when he cried
or would not sleep.  The abusive behaviour increased when child X became a
toddler, and the mother testifies that by this point, the father was repeatedly
calling child X “retarded”.  He would punish him in his room, spank him, and
out of frustration, once said that he wanted to put a knife through his head.
The mother testifies that the father made similar threats towards her,
including the threat of smashing her head against a wall.

[43]

It was at this point that the mother first
decided to leave the home and stayed in a women’s shelter for a period of three
months during which she admits to having remained in contact with the father,
who was charged for assault and uttering death threats.  The charges were
eventually dropped and the mother, accepting the father’s apology and his
undertaking to attend counselling, moved back into the family home.  Regarding
the fact that she withdrew her statement to the police in this regard, the
mother testifies that she only did so at the father’s insistence.  She adds that
once the charges were dropped, the father went back to his aggressive and
controlling ways.  She believes that no amount of counselling can change him,
that he is willing to say anything to get his way, and that he has very little
respect for authority, be it the police or otherwise.

[44]

The mother testifies that when the pandemic hit,
the father’s abusive and violent behaviour hit a peak, including towards child X
who at one point was not sent to daycare after a spanking at the hands of the
father resulting in the parents’ fear that child services would be alerted.  It
was also during this period, says the mother, that the father started holding
dirty diapers to child X’s face as a means of potty training.

[45]

The mother states that by the end of 2020, she
came to the realization that the father would not change notwithstanding
therapy and couple counselling.  She undertook to again relocate to a women’s
shelter.  A final altercation occurred between the mother and the father in
February 2021.  The police were called, and the father was removed from the
home.  Criminal charges remain pending against him as a result of this
altercation, in addition to being subject to a no contact order with the mother
and children except as otherwise permitted by the Court in the context of the
parties’ family law proceedings.

[46]

During her testimony, the mother explained that
both she and child X subsequently required trauma therapy.  She also stressed
that the father’s abusive and violent behaviour resulted in the involvement of various
victim services given the concern for the safety and well-being of both the
mother and the children.  In particular, a “High Risk Case Review” was
conducted and the mother testifies to having since established safety planning
at home and in very aspect of her family’s life out of concern that the father
will breach his no contact order, regardless of where the children may be, i.e.
at school, daycare or recreational activities.  She indicates that the father
was seen near her home in Town D and that he has also posted photos of the
children on social media in breach of the no contact order.

[47]

The mother has been in a new relationship since
2021 and has had a daughter with her new partner.  She indicates that the
children have adapted well to their baby sister and that their new family life
is positive and stable.  She indicates that the children, by choice, refer to
her new partner as “dad”, whom she describes him as a positive father figure
for the children, treating them like his own on all fronts, including
financially.  But despite having relocated and established a new family life,
the mother reiterates that she still lives in fear of the father, including the
fear of abduction.

[48]

In describing child X, the mother states that he
is still suffering from trauma symptoms and subject to emotional deregulation both
before and after supervised access visits with the father.  Specifically, she emphasizes
that he suffers from night terrors and sweats as well as headaches and
fatigue.  She adds that child X has had behavioural challenges both at home
with his brother and at school, where he can be aggressive and irritable.  She
refers to his daily struggles with his emotions, intrusive thoughts and low
self-esteem, as well as a sense that he is not allowed to cry and that his
brain is
«broken»
.  The mother notes that child X is doing
much better since having benefited from trauma therapy in February 2022.  But
she fears the long-term impact of the abuse he has suffered on his brain
development, both in terms of his brain’s physical pattern and chemical
structure.

[49]

As for child Y, the mother testifies that he has
been far less harmed by the father but emphasizes that he has not developed a
strong bond with the father and shows no interest in seeing him.  She points
out that the father’s abuse towards him was not as significant as towards child
X, in part due to child Y’s age and also because the father considered child Y
to be his «golden child».  She testifies that he was
adamant that child Y not be like child X, and that he would «get it too» when
he got older.  In connection with the supervised visits, she adds that child Y
has suffered from the father appearing to be more engaged
with child X than with child Y.

[50]

As for the children’s relationship as brothers,
the mother explains that it has been difficult in the past, with child X acting
out on child Y in the way his father did with him.  The children are now more
behaved towards one another, although the mother is fearful that maintaining
supervised visits could jeopardize this progress.

[51]

In terms of the mother’s objection to
maintaining supervised visits of the father with the children, she refers to
her 174-page “analysis of concerns” she prepared by categorizing these concerns
based on her review of the [Organisation A] and [Organisation B] reports since
supervised visits were ordered in 2021.    The categories of concerns
identified by the mother are as follows: “Defendant Shows Favoritism Among the
Children”, “Defendant Breach of No Contact Order during pick up or drop off at
visits”, “Defendant Uses Force and/or Continues Behaviour that Visibly Upsets
Children”, “Defendant Undermines the Role of the Mother and Stepfather”, “Poor
Parenting Skills by Defendant”, “Excessive Use of Gift Giving”, and “Defendant
Disrespects Facility Rules and/or Employees”.

[52]

The mother’s analysis, in her view, demonstrates
that the father remains abusive.  She considers that the father’s negative
behaviour has increased over time despite the extensive therapy he has
followed, including anger management, parental training, individual sessions
with a psychologist and meetings with Alcoholics Anonymous.  She is of the opinion
that he does not have the required personality to learn any lessons from the
past and that he reverts back to his dominant conduct when left to his own
devices.  Nothing, she says, can be done or said to reassure her, and she believes
that maintaining contact between the father and the children will only serve to
retraumatize them and would hence be detrimental.

The Father’s Testimony

[53]

At the outset of his testimony, the father explains
having been raised as an only child in a relatively violent and abusive manner,
as he puts it, indicating that he was slapped and belted by his parents.  He
refers to himself as being “rough around the edges” and “culturally different”
(he is of Jewish Romanian descent and spent part of his childhood in Israel
before moving with his parents to Canada), adding that he suffered trauma growing
up.  The father admits to having his flaws, referring to his “explosive”
nature, and acknowledges that he was verbally abusive with the mother during
their relationship (he specifically admits to having told the mother that he
wanted to throw her head against the wall) but denies any physical abuse
towards her.  He characterizes his verbally aggressive comments as
“unfortunate” and a function of his past tendency, he adds, of becoming
agitated and upset.

[54]

In terms of his parenting skills, the father
likewise admits that he struggled to contain his anger, especially when child X
was born, specifically admitting to having said that he wanted to throw him
against a wall when, at two-months old, child X was crying incessantly due to
being hungry as a result, he says, of the mother’s breastfeeding challenges.
He regrets the approach he took towards child X in terms of discipline,
admitting that his parenting may have been traumatizing for child X, including
in terms of potty training (the father testifies that putting soiled diapers to
the child’s face was only meant as a joke) and spanking (which he considers to
be different from hitting).  The father acknowledges that his behaviour cannot
be considered as “normal”, but stresses that this was how he himself was raised
as a child.

[55]

The father also admits to having consumed drugs
in the past, including cocaine, and likewise admits to having been charged with
drunk driving.  He refers to himself as an “enthusiastic partyer” but insists
that he is not addicted to anything.  He continues to suffer from anxiety and takes
medication in the form of Sertraline.  More generally, he acknowledges that he
struggled with managing the stress of becoming a parent, and feels that
circumstances, including his work schedule, prevented him from properly
developing in this regard, in contrast with the mother who he says had the
benefit of taking naps given that she worked from home.  He also acknowledges,
more generally, that he and the mother did not agree on how to discipline the
children.

[56]

In terms of the history of the father’s
relationship with the mother, he considers the mother’s account to be
exaggerated and points out that she herself comes from a mentally-ill family,
as he puts it.  The father describes the mother as sharing his sexual appetite
when they first met, and that they both had the same sexual fantasies.  He
acknowledges that their relationship became strained during the mother’s
pregnancy with child X, and apologizes for having been critical of her body
during this period and for not having been more understanding.  He feels that
the mother’s own mother did not help matters, indicating that she was very
implicated in their relationship, and highly manipulative.  He admits to having
kicked the mother’s mother out of the family home when she was visiting
following the birth of child X.  The father testifies that he has the upmost
respect for women despite the hardship and negative effects he has inflicted on
the mother.  Also, he denies ever having attempted to strangle his own mother,
as pointed out by the mother in this present matter.

[57]

The father testifies to now being a “better
person” and has attended counseling and therapy in various forms, including
therapy through a social worker during several months in 2021 as well as
multiple sessions with “Donne-toi une chance” (12 individual sessions in July
2021 and group sessions from September 2021 to May 2022).  The therapy has
been, according to the father, helpful in terms of addressing his anger
management issues, although he admits to still feeling fragile and resentful.
The father has also attended parenting classes via the CLSC and is registered
to pursue further parenting courses with “Donne-toi une chance”.

[58]

In short, the father acknowledges his parental
failings but nonetheless minimizes them by pointing out that they were not
constant, and further justifies his violent and abusive behaviour on the fact
that he and the mother were overwhelmed as parents.   He also considers that
during their relationship, the mother sought to torment and gaslight him,
especially when she was intoxicated.  Along the same lines, he takes issue with
the fact that he is always the one being accused of needing therapy as he
believes that the mother requires therapy too.

[59]

The father is currently consulting with a
therapist.  While he feels that he has learned to become a better parent and
deal with his anxiety, he continues to struggle with a sense of worthlessness,
both as a parent and as a human being, but testifies that he does not want to
give up on the children.  He emphasizes that he is their only dad and that they
need him as a father.  He adds that he misses the children and cares for them
deeply.

[60]

The father refers to himself as a realist and
understands that his relationship with the children must be approached
progressively, adding that this is why he has decided to not seek custody.  But
he believes that supervision deprives him of developing a proper relationship
with the children, especially in terms of being involved in their activities
such as soccer.  He would like to be in a position to teach them about the
things in life he enjoys, such as cooking, with a view to repairing any damage
he has inflicted upon them, adding that he has learned how to be patient, how
to talk to children and how to use positive reinforcement with them.

[61]

Finally, in terms of the father’s supervised
visits with the children, he considers that they have been going well with lots
of playtime.  He feels guilty about the turmoil he has brought on, particularly
with child X, and makes every effort to reassure him that that he did not mean
to be hurtful.  The father understands that child X is sensitive.  As for child
Y, he rejects the suggestion that he ignores him in any way during the
supervised visits.  The father considers child Y to be similar to him in terms
of being a bit of a comedian.  The father reiterates that he loves his children
and wants to be a father to them.

ANALYSIS

Preliminary
Observations

[62]

The present matter raises two main issues.
Firstly, the Court must determine whether it is in the best interest of the
children to maintain contact with the father.  If so, the Court must determine,
secondly, whether such contact should remain under supervision.

[63]

As noted, a court-ordered
psychosocial assessment has been conducted by an expert in the present matter
specifically for the purpose of assisting the Court in ruling on these
very two issues.  In essence, the expert recommends
that contact between the father and the children be
maintained, and that such contact should proceed under supervision for the time
being.

[64]

From the outset, the Court
recalls that
the
cardinal rule to be
followed in all matters involving children requires that all decisions
concerning them be made in their best interest, as set forth at article 33 of the
Civil Code states (emphasis added):

33.
Every
decision concerning a child shall be taken in light of the child’s interests
and the respect of his rights.

Consideration is given, in
addition to the moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs of the child,
to the child’s age, health, personality and family environment,
including
the presence of family violence, which includes spousal violence, or sexual
violence
, and to the other aspects of his situation.

[65]

The question of what is in the best interest of
a child is a question of fact.  It requires a weighing of various criteria,
including inter alia the needs of the child, the parents’ ability to properly
care for the child, the emotional bond between the child and the parents, the
child’s stability as well as the child’s physical and mental health.  Each case
is unique, but in all circumstances, the analysis is made with a view to
safeguarding the child’s best interest.

[66]

The purpose of the analysis is not meant to
either punish a parent or otherwise favour one parent over the other per se.  Significantly,
in a case such as the present one which involves the presence of family
violence, the Court must assess the parents’ abilities solely with a view to determining
how best to ensure that the children are protected against any determinantal behaviour.

[67]

In this regard, regardless of whether the family
violence occurs in the context of marriage or not, it is noteworthy that the
Divorce
Act
(R.S.C., 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.)) provides an insightful definition of
family violence that the Court deems useful to reproduce:

family violence
means
any conduct, whether or not the conduct constitutes a criminal offence, by a
family member towards another family member, that is violent or threatening or
that constitutes a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour or that causes
that other family member to fear for their own safety or for that of another
person — and in the case of a child, the direct or indirect exposure to such
conduct — and includes

(a) physical abuse,
including forced confinement but excluding the use of reasonable force to
protect themselves or another person;

(b) sexual abuse;

(c) threats to kill
or cause bodily harm to any person;

(d) harassment,
including stalking;

(e) the failure to
provide the necessaries of life;

(f) psychological
abuse;

(g) financial abuse;

(h) threats to kill
or harm an animal or damage property; and

(i) the killing or
harming of an animal or the damaging of property;

[68]

The
Divorce Act
expressly stipulates that family
violence must be considered when considering what is in the interest of a
child, adding that the following must be taken into account:

(a) the nature,
seriousness and frequency of the family violence and when it occurred;

(b) whether there is
a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour in relation to a family member;

(c) whether the
family violence is directed toward the child or whether the child is directly
or indirectly exposed to the family violence;

(d) the physical,
emotional and psychological harm or risk of harm to the child;

(e) any compromise to
the safety of the child or other family member;

(f) whether the
family violence causes the child or other family member to fear for their own
safety or for that of another person;

(g) any steps taken
by the person engaging in the family violence to prevent further family
violence from occurring and improve their ability to care for and meet the
needs of the child; and

(h) any other
relevant factor.

[69]

Given that the presence of family violence in this
case is admitted by the father, the Court is required to focus particularly on its
impact for purposes of ruling upon both the issue of the father’s contact with
the children and the issue of whether such contact requires supervision.  While
the Court is not bound by the expert’s findings in this regard, it is required
to give them proper weight with the understanding that in the event the Court
were to not follow the expert’s recommendations, adequate justification is
required to do so.

Is it in the children’s
best interest that contact with the father remain in place?

[70]

The expert concludes that the children should
remain in contact with their father under supervision.  She thus recommends supervised
contact notwithstanding her reservations regarding the father’s deficient
parenting skills as exacerbated by his past abusive and violent behaviour.  At
trial, the expert was questioned by the Court as to whether it should take from
this that it would be more prejudicial to the children to cease all contact
with their father than to maintain access despite his failings as a parent.  Specifically,
does the benefit for the children of maintaining contact with their father
outweigh the effect of exposing them to him in light of his past abusive
conduct?

[71]

In response to this question, the expert
reiterated that the [Organisation A] supervised visitation reports confirm that
the father has been reliable in terms of showing up to the visits and that
generally his interactions with the children are positive.  Whilst there have
been instances that illustrate the father’s need to improve his parental
abilities and develop more emotional maturity – such as when he insists on
telling the children that he is their “only” father in reference to the
mother’s new partner – he has overall demonstrated a commitment to maintaining
a bond with the children.  As for the children, the [Organisation A] supervised
visitation reports likewise confirm that with the exception of a few instances,
the visits themselves provide them with an opportunity to play, engage and
exchange with their father.  In this regard, the Court notes that the expert
had the benefit of seeing the vast majority of the [Organisation A] reports,
but not any of the [Organisation B] reports.  These remaining reports were
produced at trial and the Court, having reviewed these reports, finds that they
confirm the expert’s findings.

[72]

The more difficult aspect to determine in terms
of the children’s best interest is the impact of their contact with their
father, both before and after the visits.  In the case of child X in
particular, the impact has been observed through symptoms such as night terrors
and deregularized behaviour.  But these symptoms, while still present, have
subsided to a certain extent, in part with the assistance of trauma therapy and
also with the support and attention of the mother.  The expert considers that
provided such symptoms are dissipating – which has been confirmed by the mother
albeit with reservations – it is best that child X maintain contact with the
father, but otherwise not as this would indicate that sustained contact with
the father has a retraumatizing effect.

[73]

The expert adds that she observed a noticeable a
bond between the father and the children, i.e. both child X and child Y.
Furthermore, she considers it to be significant that the father is making an
effort to see the children, that he shows up for every visit, that good times
are had during these visits, and that it is in the interest of the children to experience
such positive interactions with their father.  She also considers it best that
the children maintain contact with the father together, as brothers, as they
have since the parties’ separation.

[74]

The Court agrees.  Had there been evidence that significant
intervention was repeatedly required during the supervised visits, or that the
children appeared consistently sad or upset during the visits, it would no
longer be in their interest to pursue these visits.  But this is not what the
visitation reports reveal.  The fact that the father has attended every single
visit over the last three years is worthy of note, as is his ongoing commitment
to continue therapy.  The mother argues that therapy has made no difference,
but she also admits that nothing could make her change her mind regarding the
father.  Such a determination requires further expert assessment, ideally on a
before and after basis to fully measure the impact of the visits on the
children, as well as the father’s progress in terms of his parenting skills.

[75]

The reality is that it would be premature at
this time to cease all contact between the father and the children.  As pointed
out by the expert, this is an exceptional case in part because the children are
of such a young age.  They cannot yet advocate for themselves and whilst some
form of contact with their father remains in principle in their best interest,
such contact cannot serve as a means of allowing the father’s past abusive and
violent behaviour to somehow be normalized again.  This is precisely the reason
why continued contact between the father and the children can only be
maintained provided that supervision remains in place.

[76]

In summary, the Court has not been persuaded
that precluding the father from any access to the children, as requested by
their mother, would be in their best interest.  Indeed, it would be more
prejudicial to the children to cut off all contact with the children than to
maintain supervised access, notwithstanding the fact that the children may
experience a degree of emotional deregulation following the supervised visits,
especially in the case of child X.  Likewise, while child Y, especially given
his age, may find his interaction with his father more challenging, it remains
in his interest to maintain at least a minimal form of contact with his father.

[77]

In terms of the frequency and length of the
contacts between the father and the children, the Court considers that in the
circumstances, it is in the best interest of the children to maintain the
status quo in this regard and that the visits should therefore continue to
proceed for two hours every two weeks.  Maintaining the status quo provides the
children with the regularity and predictability of the visits with their father
which in turn minimizes the risks and effects of any deregulation on their
part.  It also provides an opportunity to properly assess such effects,
including with the involvement of a therapist, which the Court recommends for
both children.

[78]

For these reasons, the Court accordingly
concludes that the mother’s request for a complete severance of any contact
between the children and the father should be dismissed.

Is it in
the children’s best interest that supervision remain in place?

[79]

With respect to the issue of supervision, the
expert concludes and the Court agrees that it must remain in place for the
foreseeable future given the need for the father to improve his parental skills.
To conclude otherwise, given the father’s past violent and abusive behaviour,
would put child X, who remains fragile, at risk, and would likewise put child Y
at risk as well.

[80]

Indeed, the evidence administered at trial
confirms that the father, although he admits his deficiencies as a parent, is
prone to either making excuses for his violent and abusive behaviour, such as
on account of his upbringing and the stresses of work.  And whilst he admits
that he has been violent and abusive in the past, he persists in claiming that
the mother and even the expert have chosen to exaggerate his conduct and
failings.

[81]

In principle, supervised
access is meant to be a transitional measure.  In the present case, supervised access
has been in place for nearly three years.  Nonetheless, the Court has not been
persuaded that the “transition” period for which supervised access is necessary
is complete.  Supervision remains in the children’s best interest and the Court
sees no reason to deviate from the recommendations set forth in the expert
report in this regard as well.  As the expert points out, the possibility of
eventually granting unsupervised access rights to the father is dependant upon
a timeframe that takes into account the children’s age and vulnerability.  For
the time being, there has been
a significant amount of
therapy pursued by the father but further improvement is needed to lift
supervision.  Significantly, w
hile
the father
has shown some remorse, he does not appear
to fully appreciate the impact of his past violent and abusive behaviour on the
children, which is not only a cause for concern, but in fact a risk factor
given the circumstances.

[82]

Hence, in the same way that it would be
premature at this juncture to sever all contact between the father and the
children, it would likewise be premature to lift supervision at this time as
the Court has not been persuaded the father is yet ready to proceed with
unsupervised visits.  Further progress on his part must be demonstrated before
reaching this next step, assuming it can be reached at all, which is a
determination to be made at a later time.  For the time being, supervision
provides an opportunity for continued monitoring of the father’s progress in
terms of parenting skills whilst at the same time ensuring that the children
benefit from contact with him at regular intervals in a safe and structured
environment.

[83]

For these reasons, the Court accordingly
concludes that the father’s request that supervision be lifted should be
dismissed.

Extrajudicial Costs and
Punitive Damages

[84]

The remaining issue for the Court is whether the
mother in the circumstances is entitled to extrajudicial costs and punitive
damages.  Specifically, the mother seeks 5000$ in extrajudicial costs as well
as punitive damages.

[85]

Extrajudicial costs in the nature of what is
being sought by the mother are granted in only the most exceptional
circumstances and remain subject to the Court’s discretion.  The present case
has resulted in the dismissal of both the mother and the father’s respective
requests.  Whilst the proceedings brought in advance of the trial were
significant, they were not solely attributable to the father.  Furthermore, to
grant the extrajudicial costs sought by the mother would overlook the fact that
the parties proved capable of collaborating for purposes of resolving the
financial aspects of their dispute.  For these reasons, the mother’s request
for extrajudicial costs is dismissed.

[86]

Likewise, the Court has not been persuaded that
punitive damages against the father should be ordered in this case.  Such
damages are being sought by the mother on the basis of the father’s violent and
abusive behaviour, which the Court has deemed significant for purposes of the
present family law proceedings.  But the Court cannot overlook the fact that
the criminal charges pending against the father have yet to be ruled upon,
which contrasts with the main precedent relied upon the mother in support of
her request (
2021 QCCS 3101
).  While a guilty finding regarding criminal
charges is not a perquisite to an order of punitive damages, it would appear inapposite
to make such an order in the present case.

FOR THESE REASONS,
THE COURT:

[87]

GRANTS
to the
mother exclusive parenting time of child X and child Y;

[88]

GRANTS
to the
father
supervised access to child X
and child Y, together, at the [Organisation B] located in Town D at regular
two-week intervals on Saturdays for two hours;

[89]

RECOMMENDS
that the
father pursue further therapy and parental counselling;

[90]

RECOMMENDS
that child
X and child Y be supported by a therapist for purposes of monitoring the impact
of their supervised visits with the father;

[91]

DISMISSES
the
mother’s request for extrajudicial costs and punitive damages;

[92]

Without costs.
